passage:
My worst interview? Fine, I'll tell it. I'm Francis. Two years ago my résumé said I "led the migration of the billing system". I had helped. I ran tests and wrote some documentation. My manager led it. I told myself everyone polishes, and it's only one word.
The first round went fine. In the second, the panel asked me to walk them through how I planned the timeline and handled disagreements in the team. I started talking, and about a minute in I could hear myself going in circles. One of them asked a follow-up, and I just said, "Actually, I assisted on that project." The room went quiet. I didn't get the job.
Now my résumé says "assisted". The interviews go better, because I can answer every question.

qa.q: What did Francis's résumé say two years ago?
qa.a: It said Francis "led the migration of the billing system".

qa.q: How did Francis feel when the second-round panel asked about planning the timeline?
qa.a: Francis felt panicked and exposed, hearing the answer go in circles about work Francis had not actually led.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the interview, and what did Francis choose?
qa.a: When the follow-up came, Francis admitted, "Actually, I assisted on that project", choosing honesty even though the room went quiet.

qa.q: How might the interview panel have seen Francis's answers?
qa.a: The panel likely noticed the circling answers and then the correction, and may have started doubting the rest of the résumé.

grounding: A young professional recalls turning assisted work into led work on a résumé, until interview questions exposed what could not be done.

passage:
I'm Sabina, and I sat beside Jyoti at the client pitch on Friday. Her slides said she had "designed and led" the school-lunch campaign. I remember that campaign. Our senior did the strategy; Jyoti made the posters and handled printing, and she did that part brilliantly.
The client liked the slides. Then their manager asked, "How did you choose which districts to start in?" Jyoti smiled, said, "We used data," and paused. The manager waited. I saw her hand tighten on the clicker. I stepped in and explained the survey our senior had run.
Afterwards Jyoti didn't meet my eyes. In the lift she said, "Everyone makes it sound bigger." I don't know if she believed that. She was very quiet for the rest of the day.

qa.q: What did Jyoti's slides say she had done?
qa.a: Her slides said she had "designed and led" the school-lunch campaign.

qa.q: What does Jyoti's hand tightening on the clicker suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt nervous and exposed, because she could not answer questions about work she had not led.

qa.q: What could Jyoti put on her slides next time?
qa.a: She could describe her real part, the posters and printing she did brilliantly, and credit the senior for the strategy.

qa.q: How does Sabina see Jyoti's claim?
qa.a: Sabina knows the real story, feels she had to step in to cover the gap, and isn't sure whether Jyoti believes her own excuse.

grounding: A coworker watches a young professional's inflated claim in a pitch fall apart under a simple client question.

passage:
March. Vidya updated her resume one night. Under her first job, she changed "assisted on the payments migration" to "led the payments migration." Ankita had led it; Vidya had tested screens and taken notes. Everyone polishes, she told herself.
April. The second-round interview was going well until the panel lead leaned forward. "You led the migration. Walk me through how you chose the database approach." Vidya's mind went white. She talked in circles for two minutes. The panel exchanged a look. The call ended politely.
May. Vidya opened her resume again and changed the line back: "assisted Ankita, who led the payments migration; tested all payment screens." Then she called Ankita, embarrassed, and asked if she could shadow her on the next migration to learn the part she had only pretended to know.
"Of course," Ankita said. "Bring your notes. They were always good."

qa.q: What did Vidya actually do on the payments migration?
qa.a: Vidya had tested screens and taken notes.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling when her mind went white in the interview?
qa.a: Vidya felt panicked and exposed, because the padded claim asked for knowledge she did not have.

qa.q: What did Vidya do in May to fix the problem?
qa.a: She corrected the resume line to describe her real role and asked Ankita if she could shadow her to learn the skills honestly.

qa.q: How might Ankita see Vidya's call?
qa.a: Ankita seems warm and willing to help, and appreciates Vidya's good notes, even though Vidya had claimed Ankita's lead role.

grounding: It shows a young professional inflating assisted work into led work, being exposed in an interview, and then correcting the claim over several weeks.

passage:
Sonali, you're writing a pitch deck, and I see you've written "built the whole community network." Did you? Let me, Lalremsiami, tell you something from my own first job in Aizawl.
I was twenty-four, with a small health NGO. My manager ran the village survey; I carried the forms and typed the data. When a donor visited, I introduced myself as "the person who designed our village survey." Everyone does it, I thought. It sounds better.
The donor was delighted. She asked me to present the survey method at a meeting in Shillong the following month. I spent that month in terror, reading everything my manager had written, trying to become the person I'd claimed to be.
In the end, I told my manager. She was quiet for a long moment. Then she came to Shillong with me and presented it herself. I stood beside her and did the part I had actually done.
So, Sonali. What did you build?

qa.q: What did young Lalremsiami actually do for the village survey?
qa.a: Lalremsiami carried the forms and typed the data.

qa.q: How did young Lalremsiami feel during the month before Shillong?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt terrified and ashamed, desperately reading her manager's work to become the person she had claimed to be.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped young Lalremsiami out of the trap?
qa.a: Lalremsiami told the manager the truth, and they presented together, each doing the part they had actually done.

qa.q: How might the manager have felt when Lalremsiami told her?
qa.a: The manager was probably hurt and disappointed at first, since her own work had been claimed, but she chose to help rather than expose Lalremsiami.

grounding: A senior colleague recalls turning assisted work into claimed leadership, the terror when asked to present it, and owning up.

passage:
The interview was at eleven. At ten-fifteen the power went out in the flat, the laptop was on thirty percent battery, and Rekha was reading her own resume on her phone for the tenth time.
"Managed a team of eight on the festival campaign."
She had coordinated eight freelancers' schedules in a shared sheet. Her boss had managed them.
"It's fine," said Seema, her flatmate, handing her the charger that was useless without power. "Everyone rounds up."
Rekha pictured the questions. How did you handle conflict in your team? How did you set their goals? She had no answers, only someone else's.
At eleven the call connected on low battery. After introductions, Rekha said, "Before we start, I want to correct one line. I didn't manage the team; I coordinated their schedules and deadlines. I'd rather you hear it from me."
The interviewer smiled and wrote something down. "That's useful to know. Tell me about the coordinating."

qa.q: How much battery did the laptop have?
qa.a: The laptop was on thirty percent battery.

qa.q: What was Rekha worried about as she pictured the questions?
qa.a: Rekha was worried and uneasy, knowing questions about handling conflict or setting goals would expose that she had not managed the team.

qa.q: What did Rekha choose to do, and why did it help?
qa.a: She corrected the line at the start of the call, which let her talk honestly about coordinating instead of bluffing through questions.

qa.q: How does Seema see the padded line?
qa.a: Seema sees it as ordinary rounding up that everyone does, not as a claim that could be exposed.

grounding: It shows a young professional who padded a resume, and under time pressure chose to correct it before interview questions exposed the gap.

passage:
Ira's CV said, "Led the cloud migration for a 200-person company." In truth she had assisted the lead, fixed scripts and taken notes in meetings. Everyone pads a bit, she had told herself. It's just polish.
In the glass cabin of the Bengaluru startup, Harish, the engineering head, leaned forward. "Great. Walk me through how you decided the order of the database migration."
Ira's mouth went dry. She had been in the room when that was decided. She hadn't decided it.
"We... prioritised by risk," she said.
"Which risk? And what did you do when the rollback failed on day three?"
She didn't know the rollback had failed on day three. Nobody had told her.
Ira took a breath. "I need to correct my CV. I didn't lead it. I assisted the lead. I can tell you exactly what I did."
Harish sat back. "Okay. Tell me that."

qa.q: What did Ira's CV say?
qa.a: 'Led the cloud migration for a 200-person company.'

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when Harish asked about the migration order?
qa.a: Ira felt her mouth go dry, panicked and exposed, having been in the room without making the decision.

qa.q: Why was correcting the CV in the interview the wise move?
qa.a: Harish's detailed questions were exposing the gap anyway; describing what Ira actually did gives a true picture she can defend.

qa.q: How might Harish see Ira after the correction?
qa.a: Harish seems willing to listen, 'Tell me that', and may respect the honest correction more than the padded claim.

grounding: Shows a young professional who turned assisted work into 'led' on a CV, until interview questions exposed what she could not actually explain.
